chunks.text: I think we will get started. So we're going to head back into public submissions on the Conservation Amendment Bill, and our first submitter today is Education Outdoors New Zealand, who are joining us online. Welcome, Fiona. We can see you there.

You've got 15 minutes with us this morning, so we'll take your submission as read, but we'll hand over to you for some opening remarks, and then open up for questions. So over to you. Tena koutou katoa. Thanks for the opportunity to speak to you today. I'm Fiona MacDonald, tukangunga, ngā otutao yā hau. I'm the Chief Executive for Education Outdoors New Zealand, or EONS.

EONS supports schools, careers, teachers, and outdoor providers deliver safe, high-quality outdoor education and education outside the classroom across Aotearoa New Zealand. We're here today because public conservation land is one of the most important classrooms in the country. Mm. It's where young people learn to read the weather, the rivers.

Mm. It's where they learn to walk with others, make decisions, manage uncertainty, listen to local stories, and understand ecosystem systems, and experience their own capabilities. It's where many ākonga will sleep in a tent for the first time, cross a river, hear native birds in their habitat, see stars away from city lights, and understand that conservation and restoration is not an abstract idea.

It's something they can participate in. And that's why EONS' message today, reinforcing our submission, is really simple. The Conservation Act must place conservation first. Education, recreation, and public access and enjoyment clearly sit in behind that and should always be consistent with conservation.

And commercial activity should only occur where it supports and does not limit, undermine, or displace those first two purposes. We're not opposed to commercial activity. Well-managed tourism and appropriate concessions can definitely help people access and appreciate special places. But the Act must be very clear about the order of priorities.

Public conservation land shouldn't be treated primarily as an economic development platform. If conservation is weakened, then everything that's built on it is weakened, too; outdoor education, recreation, cultural connection, community wellbeing, and the visitor economy. People don't come to Aotearoa New Zealand to see dammed rivers, industrialized wild places, demodiversity ones, come for the mountains, the amazing views, wildlife, culture and adventure, story, and the experience of being in places that feel alive. The economic benefit that comes from tourism depends

on health and integrity of nature. For schools, the environment matters in very practical ways. A teacher taking a group into a conservation area is not just taking students for a walk. They may be there to teach outdoor education through decision-making, risk awareness, leadership, and care for place. They might be teaching science through direct observation of ecosystems, PE through movement and challenge, or geography through landforms and human impact.

They may be supporting te reo Maori, mātauranga Māori through place names, pūrākau, whakapapa, and relationships with whenua and wai. Teaching citizenship by helping young people understand public good, shared responsibility, and the long-term consequences of the decisions we make about places. That learning can't be replicated fully in a classroom, on a screen, or through a worksheet. People learn differently when they're in place. They notice things. They ask different questions.

They understand scale, interdependence, and consequence in a way that's impossible to recreate indoors. Healthy, flourishing environments support healthy, flourishing people. And the opposite is true when young people grow up with reduced access to healthy places. We lose an education pathway into environmental understanding, resilience, cultural connection, confidence, and care.

And that's why EONS is asking the committee to apply an intergenerational test to this act. The question should not be what economic use can we enable now? The question should be, what will future generations inherit because of the decisions we make today? Will they inherit a healthier ecosystem?

Will they inherit access? Will they inherit places where they can still learn, explore, listen, observe, challenge themselves, and develop a lifelong ethic of care? Will mana whenua relationships with place be upheld and strengthened? Will both mātauranga Māori and ecological science inform decisions?

And will public conservation land still feel like public conservation land? If the answer's uncertain, the Act should take a proactive path. And protect conservation values. We do recognise that the system needs to be modernised. Processes can be slow, complex, and frustrating.

So we support any reform that improves clarity, efficiency, consistency and good decision-making, but it must improve how the conservation system works, not change why it exists. And our concern is with wording such as "recognise economic opportunities" and "enable the use and development to the greatest possible extent."

That's creating the wrong pull on the system. It risks asking DOC decision-makers to look for development pathways rather than first asking what the place needs in order to remain healthy or to be restored to health, be resilient in the future, and be available for public good for future generations.

Conservation land's not empty land waiting for higher economic use. It already has immense value. It holds biodiversity, whakapapa, history, identity, quiet and dark skies, wildlife, mahinga kai, stories and memories. And lots of those are values that can't be rebuilt once they're lost. They can't be offset or have a price put on them.

And therefore, we really believe that the Act needs to make the hierarchy unmistakable. Protect and enhance natural, cultural, and historic values first. Secondly, support education, public access, responsible recreation, and public enjoyment where they're consistent with conservation. And thirdly, allow tourism, commercial activity, and economic uses only where they are demonstratively consistent with conservation and do not materially compromise the above values.

The hierarchy is not anti-tourism. It's the foundation for long-term tourism. EONZ also asks the committee to give stronger attention to education as a public good outcome for conservation land. Outdoor education is one of the ways that young people become future conservation advocates.

When a student's helped planting with track care biosecurity or low-impact travel, they're not just visiting, they're learning stewardship and tiakitanga. They're learning that the outdoors is not simply a place to consume, but a place to understand, respect, care for, and return to.

And these young people, they're going to be our future teachers, parents, guides, conservation volunteers, decision-makers, community, and mana whenua leaders. If we want a society that supports conservation, young people need meaningful opportunities to experience conservation land.

So we'd like to see the removal of unnecessary barriers for not-for-profit outdoor education. Schools can undertake outdoor education on public conservation land, rightly exempt from concessions. But not-for-profit outdoor education providers delivering similar education experiences, often in partnership with schools, are still required to hold concessions.

The learning's similar, the students are similar, the places are similar, so it's hard to justify the distinction. And schools are increasingly reliant on support of these specialist outdoor providers to deliver more complex outdoor education safely. They're not commercial tourism operators seeking private gain from conservation land.

They're often charitable trusts or tertiary education organisations whose purpose is education, youth development, and wellbeing. And when concession costs, uncertainty, delays, or conditions on those programs make them less viable, the result's not better conservation. It's fewer young people learning in te taiao.

So we ask the committee to recommend adding outdoor education to the list of activities that can be carried out on conservation land without a consent, where that activity is delivered by a not-for-profit organisation. We also would ask the committee to ensure Te Tiriti o Waitangi is explicit in the Act and in the National Conservation Statement. Mana whenua relationships with place shouldn't be treated as a consultation step.

They must be part of decision-making from the beginning, and the National Conservation Policy Statement should make or should provide clear direction for mana whenua decision-making, iwi and hapū relationships with place, tikanga-led approaches to access and learning, and the use of mātauranga Māori alongside ecological science. That's not separate from outdoor education, it's central. When young people learn in places shaped by mana whenua knowledge, histories, and tikanga, they're more likely to develop respect, care, responsibility, and long-term commitment

to te taiao, the environment. And finally, we ask that access for students, schools, kura, youth organisations, and not-for-profit outdoor education providers is protected. Access to te taiao, the environment and conservation estate is an equity issue.

It's a wellbeing issue, and it's an education issue. And conservation land should never become a consumer experience available to only those who can afford it. So in closing, we ask the committee to amend the bill so that conservation remains the primary purpose for the conservation system.

We ask that education is recognised as a core public good outcome, that commercial activity is clearly subordinate and is only enabled when it generally supports conservation outcomes, that unnecessary barriers, such as requiring concessions for outdoor education providers, are removed So there's consistency between schools and not-for-profit after-education providers. And we ask the committee to take the, a long view.

The future of conservation in Aotearoa, uh, will not be secured only by rules, plans, and concessions. It's also secured by young people who know and love these places, understand their responsibilities, and can imagine themselves as kaitiaki, educators, advocates, and careful users of te— te taiao. Healthy places grow healthy people. Healthy people are more likely to care for healthy places, and the Conservation Act should protect that relationship for all our mokopuna into the future.

Thank you very much, Fiona. Um, we've just got time for a couple of questions. We'll start with Celia. Thank you very much. Thank you, Fiona. You're welcome. I'm just going to narrow down on the concession question, and, um, the cost of concessions if you've got an external provider. Do you think that that could, um, impact the safety of children because schools and parents choose the cheaper option rather than the safer option?

Yes, that's definitely one of our concerns, and also it's often, uh, the, um, conditions that are put around the concession, so they're only allowed to take a certain number of students, which limits the viability of running that program, and that's one of the concession requirements that schools don't have to face.

Thank you. So we want to reduce down those barriers so schools and students, uh, are enabled to get out there in the safest possible way. Thank you. Priyanka. Kia ora. Kia ora. Um, uh, thanks for your submission. I just have a question around the point that you've made, um, y-you've said that not all commercial activity is harmful, but the bill's direction's too broad, and you've got a, um, a few suggestions in the table around a, a hierarchy, um, and, uh, the bit that I want to ask you about is your point to remove or substan- substantially redraft

clauses that require economic opportunities to be recognized and enabled to the greatest extent practicable. Um, would removing the greatest extent practicable along with the other amendments that you've suggested be enough, or were you thinking of something else in terms of redrafting specific clauses?

Um, I think that would certainly go a ways towards, um, helping. What we're really concerned about is making sure that the priority really stays in that conservation space, and those are the key drivers around is it, um, is this activity going to improve the health, support restoration if that needs to happen?

Um, so anything that can shift and make sure the priority stays with conservation, then with education, recreation, and public access, and lastly, enabling commercial activity, whether that's tourism or other activities. Thank you. Thank you. Look, we'll take one last question from Grant McCollum.

Yeah, thank you very much. We enjoyed your presentation. Just quickly, so obviously, to enjoy the outdoors, you need, you know, good tracks, well-maintained, all that sort of thing. Um, and so you obviously recognize there is a place for having, you know, to charge, uh, appropriately for, for example, the foreign visitors, the levy we're talking about here in this case, but, and to help, to help maintain those sorts of things and to maintain economic activity where appropriate- Yes... un-underneath the conservation banner. Is that, you're okay with that?

Yes. Yes, we recognize that we need to pay for having high quality, keeping tracks safe, and enabling as much access as we can within that conservation framework. Thank you very much. Yes. Thank you very much, Fiona, for your submission and, of course, for all the work that you're doing in terms of educating our younger ones coming through.
We can all relate to our first time out in the wilderness in tents and things, so thank you very much. Um, appreciate it. Ka kite.
So our next submission this morning, um, we have Te Runanga o Ngāi Tahu are here with us in person. Welcome. Thank you.

Welcome to the select committee this morning. You have 15 minutes with us, so we'll hand over to you to open up- Kia ora... and then we'll open for questions. Thank you. Tena koutou katoa. Ngā mihi nui kia koutou. Uh, thank you, Madam Chair, uh, and members of the committee for the opportunity to appear today. I'm appearing as Chief Executive Officer of Te Runanga o Ngāi Tahu, and um, alongside me is the ōtāka pukeko Edward Allison.

Uh, this bill, uh, not only fails to deliver the new age of cooperation that has been promised to Ngāi Tahu by the Crown, but it also puts our settlement at risk. We only have 15 minutes today, and as such, I strongly encourage anyone reading this transcript or listening to these proceedings, uh, to read our submission in full, uh, where our concerns are outlined in detail.

Uh, as set out in our written submission, Ngāi Tahu has long advocated for transformative conservation reform that is modern, supports a thriving te ao Tūroa, and upholds the promises of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. The current Conservation Amendment Bill does not meet those goals, and that is why Ngāi Tahu opposes the bill.

I'll now invite Edward Allison, one of the negotiators of the Ngāi Tahu settlement, to begin. Uh, tena koe to you, Madam Chair, members of the committee. Ko Edward Allison toku iko. Uh, why conservation matters to Ngāi Tahu in, in the, in the co- settlement context. For Ngāi Tahu, conservation cannot be separated from mahinga kai.

Mahinga kai is not simply about gathering food, it reflects our identity as a people It is how our tipuna lived, traveled, traded, exercised their rangatiratanga, and related to taiao. These are not simply public conservation lands we are talking about today, or simply administrative reforms.

For us, this is about the places our tipuna occupied, named, cared for, and gathered from over countless generations. When considering this bill, we ask the committee to remember that it is making decisions that affect how the Crown recognizes and actively protects these long-standing relationships, and how it supports Ngāi Tahu rangatiratanga in our takiwā, a commitment the Crown confirmed in our Ngāi Tahu settlement.

In terms of the redress, the journey to settlement was long, and in the early 1980s, Ngāi Tahu brought together what we call the nine tall trees. Eight of those were related to the major settlements, land sales in Te Waipounamu. The ninth was related to mahinga kai.

That reflected the importance Ngāi Tahu placed on regaining access, influence, and the relationship we have with our natural environment. So by the time the negotiations occurred, much of the land within our takiwā had been passed through to the conservation estate, and in practical terms, large areas of that land were not available for return through settlement negotiations.

And as our written response states, that had a profound influence on the nature of our settlement and what that looked like. We did not seek ownership of the entire conservation estate, and instead, we negotiated mechanisms that would recognize our status as tangata whenua, and maintain our relationship and management of those places. These arrangements included taupuni, deeds of recognition, taonga species recognition, and representation on conservation boards in the New Zealand Conservation Authority, among others.

They were not incidental, those mechanisms. They were ways in which Ngāi Tahu relationship with the conservation estate was recognized where ownership could not be returned. And central to those arrangements was our understanding of Section 4 of the Conservation Act.

We understood that future conservation management decision-making would continue to be guided by a statutory obligation to give effect to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. That formed part of the foundation upon which the Crown and Ngāi Tahu rebuilt their relationship in the conservation space, and we have continued to do so to this day.

We are therefore very concerned whenever there may be an attempt to prescribe or narrow what Section 4 requires, and which we consider Section 4A, as proposed, may do. That will risk over time, that's the meaning of the Section 4, to be reduced from what it is, a powerful treaty obligation, into a procedural checklist of when iwi are to be consulted, and the time frames for that to occur. So the proposed new Section 4A does not uphold those foundations of our settlement in how the Crown must actively protect iwi,

hapū rights and interests. For the avoidance of doubt, Section 4 of the proposed bill must be removed. And I want to close by saying how disappointing it is to be here 30 years after settlement, talking about these things at this point in time.

Commitments that were made through the settlement to Ngāi Tahu, 30 years on. So Paul will now pass back to you. The key question from Ngāi Tahu is not whether conservation reform should occur, it is when and how. Our settlement and our many discussions with the Crown since then have spoken of a new age of cooperation.

It is something that we take very seriously, yet we've never seen that realized. As Edward has explained, conservation redress is a key part of the Ngāi Tahu settlement. These are solemn commitments between Ngāi Tahu and the Crown. For me, the key points this committee must consider, and which are set out in our submission are: arrangements proposed through full and final settlement are being removed without replacement.

A commitment is being made to uphold settlements and honor te Tiriti, while at the same time weakening the treaty clause. Ngāi Tahu representation that has been in place since settlement is being removed, despite local communities acknowledging its value. Decision-making is being shifted away from local communities and into centralized ministerial processes.

Collectively, these changes put our settlement at risk, put the DOC estate at risk, and diminish local and iwi voices. This is not good enough, and it is why Ngāi Tahu opposes the bill. I do not want to take up all of our time, as we're keen to answer questions, but I will finish by reiterating this.

Ngāi Tahu remains committed to the new age of cooperation that has been promised. We are ready for genuine discussions about what a new era of conservation could look like However, we are still waiting for the Crown to step up and join us at the table. Kia ora koutou, we're happy to take your questions. Thank you very much for that thorough submission.

We've got time for some questions. We'll go to Lann Farm first. Moriina koutou. Thank you so much for your submission and for being here in person. Thank you for such a clear submission. I wanted to ask about your fourth position in your written submission, because it is about a streamlined planning and concessions regime, and you're saying that as much as this bill is saying that it's going to make things better, you're interpreting it as creating unnecessary complexity, and you kind of step through the levels of

National Conservation Policy Statement area plans, past concessions, and then visitor amenity areas. Can you help the committee understand what is it within there that you think could actually be improved? And I'm noting it is a big area. So just what would be the biggest things that you think we could change, or change in these bills to help that whole situation?

Well, I think there is room for improvement in terms of reducing one layer of the plans, perhaps. Mm-hmm. Which would bring some efficiency, simplification to that. The difficulty with the proposals is that the decision making, public voice, and certainly tangata whenua voice is taken away and it is centralized.

So the decision making is centralized and takes it away from the local community, local interests. So that is a difficulty, one of the difficulties we have with it. Mm-hmm. Brown. Yeah, I'm just curious. So obviously this bill has been taking a while in the making. It hasn't just turned up.

What level of consultation and engagement have you had through this process? We engaged a huge amount with the department on a regular basis, and our kaiwhakahaere with the minister. Mm-hmm. I think part of this, though, is when I saw that two-year window that we're going to have to sort of renegotiate our treaty settlements, I was questioning whether that was actually real.

You're asking us all to renegotiate our settlements over a two-year period. So it just feels like it's just being rammed through. It's just a-- I can't see how that's quality lawmaking to do that in such a compressed timeframe. So engagement, it happens regularly, but we still want to take the time, as Edward has said, the journey that we went on over those generations.

Mm-hmm. We want to take the time to get this right for our mokopuna. Mm-hmm. Just kind of a bit of a supplementary on that. You do talk about support in principle economic use, but only where it supports, not displaces the long-term health and integrity of- Absolutely. Look- And so because obviously, it also must present a lot of opportunity for Ngāi Tahu as well, to be able to do more on the land as well.

Absolutely. For us, it's not a question of preservation and locking things up. We utilize the environment. We understand that, and we have absolute economic interest and interest in ensuring infrastructure's improved and all those elements. But it's got to be done the right way, and it's got to be done with us. As I said, new age of cooperation, that is the commitment. We want to be part of those conversations.

Not just conversations, but part of that right the way through that process. So we understand there is a significant deficit in investment in the conservation estate. We understand the challenges in biodiversity. We understand all those things you're talking about, but we want to make sure this is done in the right way. Okay. Lann. Bianca, actually. Sorry, I didn't see you there on the Zoom.

We'll go to- Thank you. I have a bit of a sup to that line of questioning around the engagement. You'd mentioned that it's not just about engagement, you want to be part of the process. Keen to better understand what that would've looked like.

And my main question is, you ended your oral presentation by saying that you don't support the bill. Keen to get a sense of whether you think, if the changes are made as you've laid out in your written submission as well, whether this is a bill that can be improved or whether you think it needs to be dispensed with and started again.

The journey we've been on has been long. When we settled, that did not magically then make that treaty compliant. It's taken us 30 years nearly, and we're building going forward. This has been a huge effort both on ourselves and for the department as well going forward. There are fundamental aspects in the bill that just will not simply work. 4A is going to undermine that very treaty relationship and really just be a transactional relationship.

Giving effect to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi takes effort, concentrated thinking, and genuine relationships. So number one, that is a huge issue with this proposed bill, is the modernization, is the Section 4, 4A. And while there has been engagement, as I say, 30 years of building on our settlement requires quite a lot of time to then engage and understand from the minister and the proposed changes, how they will work and how they will best reflect Those things that we settled in the Crown confirmed back in

1998. So some fundamental issues there with the proposed bill. The centralization of decision making will be critical. Our hapū, our iwi, at place, the ability to be sure that we'll have the appropriate level of engagement is critical. And I think my reading of Section 4A will considerably diminish that.

Thank you. Look, just one last question from Lam. Kia ora. You made it really clear about the hard won seats on the New Zealand Conservation Authority and also the conservation boards. And I'm also aware, I can't remember the terminology, but you've sort of got species representatives with Te Runanga.

Can you help the committee understand what does that look like for Te Runanga, and what do the species representatives do? The taonga species, there's a considerable schedule of them. And so there's species recovery processes. We have representation, engagement with DOC on those. On the conservation boards, we have dedicated seats, as well as having a dedicated seat on the Conservation Authority. That has been huge in terms of bringing Ngāi Tahu into the picture, being actively engaged, sitting there with public interest, because that's the public voice, very important in this

process, and also, of course, engaging with director general, minister in all aspects of conservation. They have been huge innovations going forward. Prior to settlement, we were not seen as a party, or we didn't seem to have a place. Was directly involved in developing those mechanisms because I was also on those roles, and it was a very contested place. So they've been huge in terms of building partnership, not only with DOC, but with all public participants in the conservation place. The taupēne, very important, placing their values

on special places, and quite a number of other mechanisms. There's a huge number of mechanisms. They are tools that bring us in, enable us to participate, exercise our rakitira taku in working partnership. Kia ora. Thank you. Look, thank you very much. We will have to end it there. We've met time.

We do appreciate your time today and obviously coming up in person. Really valuable discussion. So thanks for the submission. Thank you. Kia ora. Thank you. Thank you very much. Yeah. Thank you. So we now move to our next submitter, World Wide Fund for Nature New Zealand.

Who are also joining us in person today. Welcome to the committee this morning. So you have 15 minutes with us, so take your submission as read, and we'll hand over to you for your opening introductions. Thank you. Thanks. Thank you. Tēnā koutou katoa. My name's Kaitlin Owens. This is Jamie Fowler. Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today about the Conservation Amendment Bill. We want to start by saying that WWF does not support the bill in its current form.

Public conservation land and waters belong to the people of Aotearoa New Zealand. They protect some of our most important and irreplaceable natural places. They provide a home for threatened species and help sustain the natural environment that underpins so much of our economy. And let's face it, they're also what draw people in from all around the world. But these places are about more than that. Our connection to nature is part of what it means to be a New Zealander.

These places are the forests, rivers, wetlands, coastlines, and mountains where people go tramping, swimming, camping, and fishing. And as we've already seen from the incredible public response to this bill, these are the places that Kiwis want to protect and be able to pass on to our children and grandchildren. And in the midst of a biodiversity crisis, when we have one of the highest rates of species extinction in the world, around 4,000 species at risk of extinction, these places have never been more important.

The biggest problem facing New Zealand's conservation system is not that it's too difficult to develop conservation land. It is that we are losing nature at an alarming rate. For WWF, that has to be the starting point for reform. The question we should be asking is how will these changes strengthen and improve our ability to protect and restore nature?

And that's where our fundamental concern with this bill lies. Look, we do recognize there are genuine problems with the way our conservation system currently operates, and we do support the need to modernize the system. There are longstanding inefficiencies in concession processes and conservation management planning that have been a source of frustration for DOC and those who engage with it.

And we do think there's a legitimate case for reducing unnecessary administrative burden, and that there are some sensible proposals in this bill to do that. But for us, this bill goes much further than modernizing processes. It fundamentally changes New Zealand's conservation system in ways that risk weakening longstanding protections for nature. This bill elevates economic development within conservation decision-making, increases opportunities for development on conservation land, weakens public participation, and reduces independent oversight.

Ultimately, we recommend that the bill be withdrawn and substantially rewritten to ensure that conservation remains the overriding purpose of our conservation system. Our first and biggest concern is the proposed change to the purpose and direction of conservation management. The bill introduces a new function for the Department of Conservation, requiring it to recognize economic opportunities arising from conservation land and to enable that use and development to the greatest extent practicable.

We don't think that's a minor administrative change. It represents a significant shift from a conservation first framework towards one where economic development is elevated and becomes an explicit objective of the conservation system. Economic activity can already occur on conservation land through established concession processes where it's consistent with conservation objectives.

So the question is, why does economic use and development need to be elevated into an explicit function of DOC? We're concerned that doing so changes the fundamental balance of the system and risks moving us away from the system towards one where economic development becomes an objective in its own right. We're also really concerned that this provision was added in at a late stage and was not included in the proposals consulted on in February 2025.

Mm. A change with such significant implications for the department's core functions should have been subject to proper public scrutiny. In our view, this late stage change needs to be removed in its entirety. I'm now going to hand over to Jamie to talk through some of our concerns. Great. So our second concern is the way the bill creates a more development-focused framework while removing important environmental safeguards. So the proposed pre-approved and exempt activity provisions would reduce scrutiny for certain activities.

And so we understand the rationale for when you've got low risk activities, to be able to approve those more quickly. But we're concerned that the activities that have greater environmental impacts could also proceed without more robust case-by-case assessment. So particularly important here is the cumulative effect of multiple developments within these kind of areas.

An individual activity might appear relatively minor, but obviously, when you multiply activities that take place over time, there are lots of combined effects on ecosystems, species, and habitats that can be quite significant. So this is particularly concerning when nature is already under immense pressure. The provisions relating to the visitor amenity areas, in particular, also create risks of ecosystem disturbance, habitat degradation, and increased pressure on already vulnerable environments.

Again, it's the cumulative effect here that really concerns us. We're not arguing that every activity should be unnecessarily bureaucratic. We are arguing that efficiency cannot come at the expense of environmental bottom lines. So we recommend strengthening these provisions so that conservation values are maintained or enhanced and that independent ecological assessment is required where appropriate.

We should also note that we welcome the government's stated intention to remove the provisions relating to the exchange and disposal of conservation land following the outpouring of public concern. Our public conservation land shouldn't be treated as a collection of bits and bobs that can simply be traded away. Kiwis have certainly made that known. So given this issue has been well traversed, we obviously won't go into further detail on it today, other than to say we strongly support that change and encourage the committee to ensure these provisions are removed from the bill.

Our final concern is the weakening of public oversight and treaty obligations. The bill significantly increases the ministerial decision-making powers while reducing the role of the New Zealand Conservation Authority and conservation boards. These bodies provide important independent oversight and ecological expertise and community perspectives. Reducing them to largely advisory functions weakens the checks and balances and increases the risk that decisions become influenced by the short-term political considerations rather than long-term environmental

stewardship. Public conservation land and waters are a shared national treasure, and their management should reflect the values and interests of those communities they belong to. Instead, the proposed changes would narrow the circumstances in which concession applications must be publicly notified, meaning many applications could proceed without public awareness or scrutiny.

Public participation is further constrained by removing any automatic right for submitters to be heard. Hearings provide an important opportunity, obviously, to test evidence and ensure decision-makers hear directly from affected communities and stakeholders. We're also concerned that some of the provisions around treaty obligations and Māori engagement risk reducing what is currently the strongest obligation to give effect to treaty principles into something more like a procedural checklist.

You would have heard this obviously from Matua Edward Ellison in the previous submission. Mātauranga Māori and Māori stewardship approaches provide critical insights into long-term ecosystem health and biodiversity protection. At its core, effective conservation depends on ensuring enduring partnerships and shared stewardship. Meaningful engagement with treaty partners is not simply a procedural requirement, it is fundamental to achieving conservation outcomes, and that these outcomes are durable and they're equitable, and they're

reflective of Aotearoa's unique context. We therefore recommend restoring stronger notification and hearing rights, strengthening the roles of conservation boards and NZCA, and ensuring early, meaningful, and properly resourced iwi and hapū engagement with greater opportunities for Māori leadership in conservation decision-making.

Ultimately, we think the conservation system works best when decisions are informed by strong science, independent oversight, public participation, and genuine partnership with Tangata Whenua. To conclude, WWF agrees that Aotearoa, New Zealand's conservation system needs modernization. We support better processes, greater efficiency, and removing unnecessary barriers to effective conservation management.

But this bill goes much further than that. So it changes the direction of our conservation system in ways that risk weakening protections for nature. As Caitlin mentioned, at a time when we're facing a biodiversity crisis, we need reforms that actually strengthen our ability to protect and restore nature, not make it easier to develop the places we're already struggling to protect.

Reform of this magnitude must be grounded in a clear and unwavering commitment to protect our biodiversity, maintaining ecological integrity, and upholding the public interest. The decisions here will determine what is left for the next generation. The rivers, the forests, the wetlands, the coastlines, and mountains we protect today are the places future generations should still be able to know and explore and love.
